_comment: Grading machines; rsi_loop.prepare() puts the one named by the run's config.json "grade_on" into each round's instruction.md (GRADER_SHORT, GRADER_MACHINE). Add one here before switching a run to a new machine. "machine_gcp": the same text for rounds whose agent works on the GCP VM (CPU only; rsi_loop.prepare(where="gcp"), from 2026-11-10).

ls6.short: one NVIDIA A100 GPU (40 GB, CUDA) on a TACC Lonestar6 Linux node
ls6.machine:
- **This round the grader runs your program on one NVIDIA A100 (40 GB, CUDA, `device="cuda"`)** on a TACC
  Lonestar6 Linux node, with 8 CPU threads; keep host memory under about 32 GB. Python 3.12 with numpy 1.26, scipy
  1.13, astropy 6.1 and torch 2.11 (CUDA 12.8) only (no matplotlib there). Write the program for the A100: CUDA
  tensors, float32 or TF32 where precision allows (float64 is several times slower on an A100), large batched kernels
  rather than Python loops.
- **You write and test here, on an Apple M1 Ultra** (48-core GPU through `device="mps"`, 64 GB unified memory shared
  with the system; use at most 4 CPU threads). `~/anaconda3/bin/python` has the same packages with MPS instead of CUDA
  (MPS has no float64). There is no CUDA here, so the same code must pick `cuda` when available, else `mps`, else `cpu`,
  and avoid CUDA-only features you cannot test (custom CUDA kernels, Triton). Timings here are only a rough guide to
  the A100's. No network, and you cannot install packages.
ls6.machine_gcp:
- **This round the grader runs your program on one NVIDIA A100 (40 GB, CUDA, `device="cuda"`)** on a TACC
  Lonestar6 Linux node, with 8 CPU threads; keep host memory under about 32 GB. Python 3.12 with numpy 1.26, scipy
  1.13, astropy 6.1 and torch 2.11 (CUDA 12.8) only (no matplotlib there). Write the program for the A100: CUDA
  tensors, float32 or TF32 where precision allows (float64 is several times slower on an A100), large batched kernels
  rather than Python loops.
- **You write and test here, on a Linux virtual machine with no GPU**: 16 CPU threads and about 48 GB of memory
  for your whole session, shared by all your test runs (other people's jobs also run on this machine). `~/anaconda3/bin/python`
  has the grader's packages for the CPU (numpy 1.26, scipy 1.13, astropy 6.1, torch 2.11 CPU build) plus matplotlib.
  There is no GPU here, so the same code must pick `cuda` when available, else `mps`, else `cpu`, and avoid
  CUDA-only features you cannot test (custom CUDA kernels, Triton). Torch runs on the CPU here: test runs are much
  slower than on the A100 and get less done within the same budget, so timings here are only a rough guide to the
  A100's. Until gen013 the agents worked on an Apple M1 Ultra GPU (`mps`); timings in earlier notes were measured
  there. No network, and you cannot install packages.

mac.short: this Mac (Apple M1 Ultra GPU through MPS)
mac.machine:
- **This round the grader runs your program on this Mac**: Apple M1 Ultra, 48-core GPU through PyTorch
  (`device="mps"`, no float64), 64 GB unified memory shared with the system; at most 4 CPU threads, keep memory under
  about 32 GB. Python: `~/anaconda3/bin/python` (numpy, scipy, astropy, torch with MPS, matplotlib). No network, and
  you cannot install packages. Pick `cuda` when available, else `mps`, else `cpu`, so the code also runs on NVIDIA GPUs.
